paragraphs: Sumer supplies the earliest known abacus, somewhere between 2700 and 2300 BCE, a table ruled into columns, each column standing for a place in the Sumerians' base sixty counting system. It let a merchant or scribe track quantities that were awkward to hold in the head alone.

Babylonian cuneiform may preserve a sign derived from that same counting board, and later Babylonian scholars are thought to have used similar devices for simple sums, though the tool struggled once the arithmetic grew complex. The Sumerian table remains the firmer, earlier fixed point in the record.

Farming did not start once. It began independently in at least half a dozen regions after the last Ice Age ended, roughly 11,700 years ago. The Fertile Crescent was first, around 10,000 to 8,000 BCE, where people began tending einkorn and emmer wheat, barley, lentils and flax rather than only gathering them wild.

Within a few thousand years the same shift happened separately in the Yellow and Yangtze river basins in China, in the Ethiopian highlands and West Africa, in Papua New Guinea with taro, and later in Mesoamerica with maize, beans and squash. Each population arrived at cultivation on its own crops, with no single point of origin behind the change worldwide.

Alexander beat King Porus at the Hydaspes River in 326 BC, in what is now Punjab, and reportedly wanted to keep marching east toward what he believed was the edge of the world. His army disagreed: after years away from home and eight years of continuous campaigning, they refused to go further.

The mutiny stopped him at the Beas River. Alexander turned back toward Babylon, where he died in 323 BC without seeing the rest of the subcontinent he had set out to reach, and the empire he had built split among his generals within a few years of his death.

The clearest fossils for this stage come from Jebel Irhoud in Morocco: skull, jaw and limb bones from at least five individuals, dated by heating stone tools found alongside them to roughly 315,000 years old, with a possible range of 280,000 to 350,000. The jawbone shows an inverted T shaped chin, a feature typical of living humans rather than older hominins.

The skulls are not fully modern even so. Their faces already look close to ours, but the braincase behind them is still long and low rather than the rounded shape typical today, meaning brain shape kept changing within the species for tens of thousands of years afterward. The find also pushed the known record of this transition further back and further west than earlier evidence had shown.

Ancient writers credited Anaximander of Miletus as the first person to publish a map of the known world, placing the Aegean at its centre and showing Europe, Asia and Libya as islands ringed by ocean. The Nile was drawn running south, marking the boundary between Libya and Asia.

No copy survives. Everything known about it comes from later Greek writers who described it rather than reproduced it, and it likely inspired a more detailed version by the historian Hecataeus of Miletus. Historians think Anaximander drew it to aid Ionian trade and shipping as much as to record geography for its own sake.

Earlier bridge builders had used flat beams or simple corbelling, both limited in span and load. Roman engineers cut wedge-shaped voussoirs of matching size and set them in a semicircle so the whole arch pushed its weight sideways into the banks, letting a single span cross wider water and carry far heavier traffic than a beam could bear.

A later survey counted 931 Roman bridges still traceable across twenty-six countries. The Pons Fabricius in Rome, built in 62 BC, still carries pedestrians, and the same arch principle carried water across valleys on aqueducts such as the Pont du Gard, with openings built into the piers to let floodwater through.

A Syracusan king asked Archimedes to check whether his new crown was pure gold or cut with silver, without damaging it. The bathtub scene and the shout of eureka come from a much later account and are not confirmed by any source close to Archimedes' own lifetime, so the famous version of the story rests on shaky ground.

The method that actually follows from his surviving work is quieter: balance the crown against an equal weight of pure gold on a scale, then lower both into water together. A crown diluted with a lighter metal would displace more water and tip the scale, revealing the fraud without melting anything down.

No single inventor's name survives attached to the astrolabe. Theon of Alexandria wrote a detailed treatise on it in the fourth century, and later legend credited his daughter Hypatia, though that claim is not well supported. A metal disc engraved with wires and sight lines, it let its user read the position of the stars against the time of day.

The instrument travelled into the Islamic world, where the earliest surviving example dates to the tenth century and one astronomer catalogued over a thousand uses for it: fixing prayer times, finding the direction of Mecca, surveying land, and telling time by the sun or stars long before mechanical clocks existed.

Balboa set out across the Isthmus of Panama on 1 September 1513 with roughly 190 Spaniards, indigenous guides and dogs. On 25 September, ahead of the rest of his party, he climbed a ridge along the Chucunaque River and became the first European recorded to see the ocean that lay beyond the Americas.

It did not save him. A new governor, Pedro Arias de Avila, arrived, and though Balboa married his daughter the peace did not last. In 1519, Francisco Pizarro arrested him on charges of treason, and Balboa was beheaded at Acla still protesting his innocence.

Vitus Bering, a Dane serving under Peter the Great, sailed north through the strait that now carries his name in July 1728, watching the Siberian coast bend away to the west. He asked his officers whether that turn meant Asia had run out of land to the east.

Fog kept the Alaskan shore out of sight the whole voyage, so Bering came home with strong evidence rather than proof, and doubts about whether the continents were truly separate lingered among geographers. He also had no way of knowing that the Russian explorer Semyon Dezhnev had sailed the same passage some eighty years earlier.

Excavated Chinese blast furnaces go back at least to the first century BC, under the Han dynasty, centuries before similar furnaces appeared in Europe. Where a bloomery only produced a spongy lump of iron, a blast furnace ran hot enough to melt it fully, yielding a liquid that could be cast directly into moulds for tools and weapons.

The engineer Du Shi later harnessed waterwheels to drive the bellows that fed these furnaces, letting a river do the work of pumping air instead of labourers. By the eleventh century, Song ironworks had also switched from charcoal to coke, sparing large tracts of woodland from being cut for fuel.

The bow is far older than farming. Small stone points from Obi-Rakhmat Grotto in Uzbekistan, sized wrong for a spear and too heavy for a blowgun dart, carry impact damage consistent with arrow use and have been dated to around 80,000 years ago. Similar points from Sibudu Cave in South Africa and Mandrin Cave in France push the technology back tens of thousands of years before the end of the last Ice Age.

What changed after the ice retreated, around 12,000 years ago, was reach rather than invention: the bow spread into nearly every inhabited region except Australia and most of the Pacific islands. Wood and sinew rarely survive that long, so almost everything known about its earliest use comes from stone points alone, not the bows themselves.

The apparatus behind Boyle's 1662 law was a simple bent glass tube, closed at one end and open at the other, into which mercury was poured. As the mercury rose on the open side, it squeezed the trapped air in the closed end into a smaller space, and Boyle could read off both the pressure and the resulting volume from marks on the glass.

Several historians credit the tube itself to Boyle's assistant, Robert Hooke, who built and refined the apparatus in Boyle's laboratory. The result, that a gas's pressure rises exactly as its volume falls when temperature stays fixed, held for the modest pressures Boyle could test and became one of the earliest laws of physical science expressed as a precise ratio.

Louis Braille lost his sight as a small child after an accident with an awl in his father's leather workshop spread infection to both eyes. At the Royal Institute for Blind Youth in Paris he learned of a military code called night writing, devised by Charles Barbier so soldiers could read orders in the dark without a lamp.

Barbier's system used up to twelve raised dots per character, too many to feel under one fingertip at once. Braille cut it down to a six dot cell that a single finger could read in one touch, and presented the finished system to his classmates in 1825, when he was fifteen.

Copper alone is too soft for a lasting edge, and the fix was not obvious: alloying it with tin required mining and smelting a second, much rarer metal, then combining the two while the copper was hot. The Maykop culture of the North Caucasus was working an arsenic bronze by the mid fourth millennium BCE, and a disputed tin bronze foil from Serbia may push true tin alloying back even further.

Tin occurs in only a handful of places, so early bronze stayed scarce and expensive long after the technique was known. Many communities kept using stone tools for everyday work and reserved bronze for weapons and the objects of people with the authority to command a long supply chain for the tin alone.

The Nihon Shoki records that King Seong of Baekje sent Emperor Kinmei a bronze image of the Buddha, banners and sutras, an act later chronicles date to 552, though some sources give 538 instead. Kinmei asked his court whether the foreign faith should be honoured, and the court split rather than agreed.

The minister Soga no Iname argued for worship; the Mononobe and Nakatomi clans warned that Japan's own kami would take offence. Kinmei let the Soga clan alone test it privately, and opponents are said to have thrown the Buddha image into a canal in protest. The Soga faction eventually prevailed by force, and Buddhism spread with the court's backing after that.

Buddhism reached China from Central Asia sometime around the first century AD, carried along trade routes by monks and merchants rather than by any single missionary. Exactly when the first teachings arrived is not recorded precisely, but Han-dynasty court circles were already discussing the faith within decades of its arrival.

Among the earliest documented figures is An Shigao, a translator who rendered Buddhist texts from Sanskrit into Chinese so that scripture could circulate beyond a handful of bilingual scholars. That translation work, more than any single conversion, is what let the religion take root far from the trade routes that first carried it.

John Cabot made landfall on 24 June 1497, sailing for Henry VII of England, but where he actually stepped ashore is unresolved. Historians have argued for sites across Newfoundland, Cape Breton, Labrador and Maine; Cape Bonavista was chosen only as an official marker for the 500th anniversary in 1997.

His next voyage, five ships out of Bristol in May 1498, simply vanished from the record. Nobody knows whether Cabot died at sea, returned and died soon after, or stayed in the Americas; one crewman, Lancelot Thirkill, later turns up alive in London, which is nearly all that is known of the outcome.

Cabral left Lisbon on 9 March 1500 with thirteen ships bound for India by the sea route da Gama had just opened, and reached the coast of what is now Brazil on 22 April, at a hill he named Monte Pascoal. Whether that landfall was a planned detour or a genuine accident of currents is still argued; no surviving document settles it either way.

He judged the coastline too large to be an island, claimed it for Portugal under the Treaty of Tordesillas, exchanged gifts with the people he met there, and had a wooden cross raised before sending a ship home to report the find and continuing on to India.

Objects once read as candlesticks in Tutankhamun's tomb probably were not candles at all, and the earliest artificial light was simply an open fire or a torch, followed by wicks floating in pools of oil or fat, a method reaching back to the Paleolithic. A true dipped candle, wax or tallow built up around a fixed wick, is a later refinement of that older floating-wick lamp.

The clearest early trace of a candlestick as an object comes from Etruscan Italy: a depiction survives in a tomb at Orvieto, and an excavated Etruscan candlestick has been dated to the seventh century BCE. Rome later made dipped candles from tallow and beeswax in large enough numbers that they show up routinely in the archaeological record.

At Gaspe Bay in July 1534, Cartier raised a ten-metre cross reading 'Long live the King of France' and planted it as a territorial claim. The Iroquoian chief Donnacona, whose land it was, objected, and Cartier answered by taking Donnacona's two sons aboard his ship for the return voyage.

The chief seems to have accepted the loss on the understanding the young men would come back with French trade goods, and they did sail home with Cartier the following year. Cartier returned to France that September believing, wrongly, that the coastline he had charted belonged to Asia.

Diodorus Siculus lists the device as part of a Greek army's equipment in 399 BC, built for Dionysius I of Syracuse, who was tightening his hold on Sicily against Carthage. It worked on tension, like an oversized crossbow, rather than the twisted-rope torsion springs that later versions used.

Within a few decades Greek engineers had switched to torsion power, storing energy in tightly wound cords of sinew or hair for a harder throw. An Athenian inscription from the late 330s BC is the earliest clear record of that switch, and the design stayed the basis of siege artillery for centuries afterward.

Surviving mail is oldest in the Carpathian Basin, dating to the third century BC, though pattern mail from Etruscan graves may be a century older still. Its invention is usually credited to Celtic smiths, who hammered wrought iron into wire, cut it into rings, and linked each one to four neighbours before closing the joins with a rivet.

Rome met mail on the battlefield rather than inventing it: after fighting Gallic warriors in northern Italy, Roman armies adopted it as the lorica hamata. From there it travelled with traders and soldiers into North Africa, the Middle East, Central Asia and eventually Japan, where by the fourteenth century it had become part of samurai equipment.

The claim comes from a single 2002 book, 1421: The Year China Discovered the World, by Gavin Menzies, a retired British submarine officer with no formal training as a historian. He argued that Admiral Zheng He's treasure fleets reached the Americas decades before Columbus and circled the globe before Magellan.

Historians reviewed the case and rejected it outright. Robert Finlay called its reasoning circular and its evidence spurious, and a group of international scholars issued a joint statement describing the book as fiction presented as revisionist history, noting that no document or artefact has ever supported it.

Lydia, in what is now western Turkey, struck the earliest coins from electrum, a natural alloy of gold and silver panned from local riverbeds. Because the gold content varied so wildly, some pieces carried far less value than they appeared to, which pushed Lydian mints toward stamping each coin to guarantee its weight and origin.

Attribution is uncertain: the coinage is most often credited to King Alyattes, who died around 560 BC, though some scholars push it back to his predecessor Gyges. The earliest pieces were not even standardised in weight, and may have started as temple badges rather than money for everyday trade.

Land was sighted before dawn. Columbus made landfall on an island the Lucayan people called Guanahani, in the Bahamas, and renamed it San Salvador. He went on to Cuba and Hispaniola, where he left men behind at a settlement called La Navidad.

He never accepted that he had found a new continent. His own letters insist he had reached Asia, and he held to that claim through three further voyages made between 1493 and 1504, each funded by the Crown of Castile and each pushing further into land he still described as the edge of the Indies.

The first magnetic compasses in Han-dynasty China were not built for finding direction at sea. Carved from lodestone into a spoon-shaped south-pointing fish, they were used for geomancy, orienting buildings and burial sites according to the principles of feng shui rather than plotting any journey.

Sailors did not take up the needle until centuries later: land forces used a compass for navigation before 1044, and the earliest surviving account of ships steering by a south-pointing needle in poor visibility dates to between 1111 and 1117, during the Song dynasty, roughly a thousand years after the instrument's first divinatory use.

A single pulley only changes the direction of a pull, not its force. Running the same rope through several wheels, each supporting part of the load, lets one hand do the work of many by trading distance pulled for force applied, the same trick behind Hero of Alexandria's later crane designs and still the working principle of a block and tackle today.

Ancient writers credited Archimedes with building such rigs to lift weights no team of labourers could manage alone, work that grew out of his broader study of levers and centres of gravity in third-century Syracuse. The device survives mainly through later description rather than any of his own surviving texts on the subject.

Cortes reached the Aztec capital, Tenochtitlan, on 8 November 1519, and Moctezuma II received the Spanish peacefully and gave them gold. The gift did the opposite of satisfying his visitors and sharpened their interest in the city's wealth.

Moctezuma had allowed Cortes in deliberately, intending to learn the Spaniards' weaknesses before moving against them. Word then reached Cortes that Spaniards on the coast had been killed by Aztec forces, and he responded by seizing Moctezuma in his own palace, ruling the city through him as a hostage.

Cast bronze crossbow locks found in China have been dated to around 650 BC, and bronze bolts from a similar period have turned up in a burial in Hubei province. Unlike a longbow, which takes years of practice to draw with any power, a crossbow could be aimed and fired competently after brief training.

That made it possible to arm huge conscript armies quickly. Han dynasty soldiers were required to draw a bow rated at roughly 76 kilograms to qualify, and armies fielded crossbows in the tens and later hundreds of thousands, making the weapon standard issue rather than a specialist's tool.

Cyril and Methodius, sent from Byzantium to bring Slavic liturgy to Great Moravia, devised the Glagolitic script for it, a set of letters unrelated to the Greek or Latin alphabet. Cyrillic came after them: their students at Bulgaria's Preslav literary school built a new script by adapting Greek uncial letters instead, under Tsar Simeon the Great.

Preslav scholars, trained on Greek models, dropped Glagolitic's odd loops within a generation in favour of the more familiar looking Cyrillic. The earliest surviving Cyrillic inscriptions date to around 921, near the Bulgarian village of Krepcha, and the script later carried Slavic literacy from the Balkans into Russia.

John Dalton was a Manchester schoolteacher studying the weather when he started asking why gases in a mixture behave as if each were alone in the container. Around 1803 he began arguing that matter is made of indivisible atoms, each element having its own fixed weight, and that compounds form when atoms combine in simple whole-number ratios.

He got some of those ratios wrong: lacking any way to count atoms directly, he guessed water was one hydrogen atom to one oxygen, not two to one. The core idea held anyway, and he set it out fully in A New System of Chemical Philosophy in 1808, giving chemistry its first table of relative atomic weights.

Captain Robert FitzRoy wanted a gentleman naturalist aboard, someone to talk to on the long voyage as much as to examine rock and specimen. Cambridge professors recommended a 22 year old graduate named Charles Darwin, who paid his own way and held no official post on the ship.

HMS Beagle left Plymouth on 27 December 1831 on a survey expedition meant to last two years; it did not return until October 1836. Darwin spent most of that time on land, only about eighteen months actually at sea, filling notebooks with observations of rock strata, fossils and living species across South America and the Pacific.

De Soto had no interest in the river he reached in May 1541. To him it was simply an obstacle blocking a march he had already spent two years on, and his men spent roughly a month building flatboats before ferrying the expedition across at night to avoid the Native patrols watching the banks.

The crossing point is disputed. A 1935 federal commission favoured Sunflower Landing in Mississippi, though later researchers have argued for sites as far off as Memphis. De Soto died of fever the following year, and his men sank his body in the river by night to hide his death from people he had told them he could not die among.

On 4 February 1488, after thirty days at sea, Bartolomeu Dias reached Mossel Bay on Africa's southern coast and watched the shoreline turn northeast, proof that the continent had an end. He wanted to keep sailing towards India.

His officers overruled him. Supplies were low and the ships were battered, so the crew voted to turn back, and Dias agreed. The return route he worked out, looping far out into the open Atlantic before cutting east, was the one Vasco da Gama later used to reach India himself.

What William Buckland had was fragments: part of a lower jaw with a tooth still in it, some vertebrae, ribs, pieces of a pelvis and a thigh bone, gathered from a Oxfordshire quarry over several years. No complete skeleton has ever been found for this species, and he never saw the animal whole.

He named it Megalosaurus, 'great lizard', and described it to the Geological Society of London on 20 February 1824. The word dinosaur did not exist yet. Richard Owen coined it in 1842, using Megalosaurus as one of three genera that defined the new group, which is why this pile of fragments counts as the first dinosaur ever named.

Dionysius Exiguus was a monk from Scythia Minor working in Rome, compiling Easter tables for the pope. The tables he inherited numbered years from the reign of Diocletian, an emperor remembered in the church for persecuting Christians, and Dionysius wanted a count that did not honour him.

So he renumbered the years from the incarnation of Christ instead, without ever stating in his surviving text exactly which year he meant. Later readers reconstructed it as 1 BC. He never learned the count would outlast the Easter tables it was built for: modern scholarship, working from Herod's death, puts the birth several years earlier than his figure.

Cattle come from the aurochs, a wild ox that once ranged across Europe, Asia and North Africa and stood taller at the shoulder than any modern breed. Genetic evidence suggests the main domestic line traces back to as few as eighty tamed animals in upper Mesopotamia, in the area that is now Turkey and Syria, roughly 10,500 years ago.

That was not the only time it happened. A separate, later domestication in the region that is now Pakistan produced the humped zebu line still dominant across South Asia and the tropics today, and some researchers argue for a third, African domestication distinct from both. The aurochs itself survived the split: the last wild individual died in Poland in 1627.

For years the leading candidate for first domestication was the Botai culture of Kazakhstan, where worn teeth and milk residue on pottery pointed to riding and milking on the steppe. Genetic testing later found that Botai horses left almost no trace in modern bloodlines, so that population was a separate, dead-end domestication rather than the ancestral one.

Genome studies of hundreds of ancient horses now trace nearly all living domestic horses to the Volga-Don region of southern Russia, spreading outward with chariot burials at sites such as Sintashta. The steppe origin survives the correction even though the exact culture and centuries keep moving as older bones and new genomes are tested.

The donkey descends from the African wild ass, most directly its Nubian and Somali subspecies, and the earliest domestic remains come from Ma'adi in Lower Egypt, dated to the fourth millennium BCE. By Egypt's Fourth Dynasty, around 2675 to 2565 BCE, wealthy households are recorded owning over a thousand of them, used for farm work, dairy, meat and carrying loads.

Their advantage over cattle for trade was practical rather than glamorous: donkeys do not need to stop and chew cud, so a laden train could keep moving. By the end of the fourth millennium BCE the animal had spread into Southwest Asia, and by 1800 BCE the main breeding centre for donkeys had shifted to Mesopotamia.

Pigs were tamed from wild boar twice over, in two places that never had contact with each other. The earlier event was in the Tigris basin in the Near East, around 11,400 years ago, evidenced by pig remains on Cyprus that must have arrived by boat from the mainland. A second, unrelated domestication followed in China roughly 8,000 years ago.

The two lines did not stay separate. When Near Eastern pigs reached Europe they interbred repeatedly with local wild boar, so much so that modern European pig genomes carry less than five percent of their original Near Eastern ancestry, yet the animals kept every trait that makes a pig domestic rather than wild. Descent, in this case, turned out to matter less than selection.

Sheep descend from the Asiatic mouflon and were domesticated in Mesopotamia between roughly 11,000 and 9000 BCE, before the practice spread east to Mehrgarh in the Indus Valley by about 7000 BCE. Wool was not the point at first: early flocks were kept for meat, milk and skins, the same reasons any animal got penned in rather than hunted.

Deliberate breeding for a woolly coat only shows up around 6000 BCE, and the earliest surviving woven wool cloth dates to about 4000 BCE, some two thousand years after the animals themselves were first kept. Fleece, in other words, was a slow-arriving bonus on top of an animal already valued for its meat and its milk.

Earth is estimated at about 4.54 billion years old, with an uncertainty of roughly one percent. It grew inside a flattened disc of dust and gas circling the young Sun, as smaller clumps of debris collided and stuck together in a process called accretion. Some models suggest the bulk of this assembly took only a few million years, far faster than once assumed.

The date rests on radiometric dating of meteorites and Moon rock rather than any Earth rock, since plate tectonics has recycled almost all of the original crust. The oldest surviving fragments are zircon crystals from Australia, about 4.4 billion years old, and their chemistry hints that oceans already existed soon after the crust cooled.

In 1831 Faraday wound two insulated coils around opposite sides of an iron ring and found that switching current on in one coil briefly pushed a current through the other, even though the two wires never touched. Sliding a magnet through a simple loop of wire produced the same effect, a moving field driving current in the loop.

This was electromagnetic induction, the reverse of what his motor experiment a decade earlier had shown. Faraday went on to build a working generator from the same principle, the ancestor of the dynamos that would eventually turn mechanical motion into the electricity supplying homes and factories, though that practical shift was still decades away.

Faraday's 1821 apparatus was little more than a cup of mercury, a fixed magnet standing in it, and a wire hanging free above. Current running through the wire made it swing round and round the magnet without ever touching it, converting electrical current directly into continuous mechanical motion for the first time.

He wrote the result up and sent small working models to colleagues across Europe rather than keeping the discovery to himself. It would be decades before motors built on the same principle did useful work, but every later design, from tram engines to kitchen appliances, traces its operating idea back to that spinning wire.

William Sturgeon built his magnet from eighteen turns of bare copper wire wound around a curved iron core. Insulated wire did not exist yet, so the turns had to be spaced to keep the bare metal from touching itself and shorting the current, a fiddly limit on how strong the coil could be made.

He demonstrated the result by lifting nine pounds of iron with a seven ounce core, current from a single battery holding the load until he switched it off. Unlike a permanent magnet, his could be turned on and off at will, and that switchable pull became the working principle behind electric bells, relays and eventually electric motors.

No inventor's name survives with certainty. A Dominican friar, Giordano da Pisa, told a congregation in 1306 that spectacles were less than twenty years old and that he had met the man who first made them, without recording who that was.

A Pisan friar named Alessandro della Spina is credited only with sharing the technique freely once he learned of it, and a later claim that a Florentine named Salvino degli Armati invented glasses has since been shown to be false. Venice had a spectacle makers' guild by 1320.

Using fire and making it are two different skills with two different timelines. Charred bones deep inside Wonderwerk Cave in South Africa, out of reach of any wildfire, put fire use back around 1.79 million years, well before Homo sapiens existed. The oldest strong evidence for actually starting a fire on demand is far younger: baked earth with flint and pyrite at Barnham in England, roughly 400,000 years old.

Cooking sits somewhere between the two. Heated fish teeth from a cave by the Sea of Galilee, about 780,000 years old, are among the earliest signs that food was being deliberately warmed rather than eaten raw. Some researchers push cooking back much further, to 1.8 million years, based on changes in fossil teeth, but that claim has limited support among specialists.

Homo sapiens emerged in Africa at least 300,000 years ago from a population usually classed as Homo heidelbergensis or Homo rhodesiensis. There was no single founding moment: the change from one species to the other is a matter of gradually accumulating traits across scattered African populations, reconstructed from a handful of fossils rather than an unbroken record.

Those first populations stayed in Africa for a long stretch before spreading elsewhere. Genetic and fossil evidence points to at least two later waves leaving the continent, one around 130,000 to 100,000 years ago and a second, larger dispersal about 70,000 to 50,000 years ago, during which sapiens met and sometimes interbred with other human species already settled abroad.

No fossil marks the first living cell. The strongest direct evidence is a set of stromatolites, layered mounds built by microbial mats, found in Western Australia's Dresser Formation and dated to about 3.5 billion years ago. Some researchers argue for life as early as 4.1 billion years, based on a single zircon grain carrying a carbon signature associated with living things.

That older claim stays contested, because the same chemical signature can, in principle, form without biology at all, through volcanic or hydrothermal reactions. Even the stromatolites face the same objection from some geologists. The debate is less about whether early Earth could host life than about how confidently a single ancient rock can prove it did.

Nyayanga in Kenya has yielded the oldest confirmed stone tool industry, the Oldowan, dated to about 2.9 million years ago, with a possibly distinct and even older set of tools from Lomekwi at roughly 3.3 million years. Nobody knows for certain which species made them. At Nyayanga the flakes turned up alongside butchered hippo bones, and beside teeth from Paranthropus rather than any Homo species.

That ambiguity matters, because the tools have long been credited to a single toolmaking lineage leading to us. Cut marked bones found with tools at Gona in Ethiopia, about 2.6 million years old, show the same basic technique was already spread across East Africa, used for stripping meat and marrow rather than shaping anything ornamental.

Twenty three Jewish refugees from Dutch Brazil landed in New Amsterdam in September 1654 and were grudgingly allowed to settle a year later. For decades their congregation, Shearith Israel, worshipped in rented rooms rather than a public building of its own.

That changed on Mill Street in lower Manhattan in 1730, when the congregation dedicated its first purpose built synagogue. It remained the only synagogue in New York City for nearly a century, and Shearith Israel is still counted the oldest Jewish congregation in the country.

Earlier flush toilets, including a design John Harington had built two centuries before, solved waste removal but left an open pipe running straight back to the sewer, and the smell followed it into the house. Cumming, a watchmaker and instrument maker by trade rather than a plumber, bent the outlet pipe into an S shape.

Water settled permanently in the curve of that S and blocked the gases behind it, which is still how a toilet trap works today. His 1775 patent also linked the inlet valve to the flush handle so a single pull both emptied the bowl and refilled it, a mechanism closer to a clockmaker's linkage than a builder's fitting.

No bolt struck the kite. What the popular version leaves out is that Benjamin Franklin's kite drew a charge simply by flying near a storm cloud in June 1752, with his son William holding the line beside him. Franklin noticed loose threads on the string standing apart from each other, the sign that it had become charged.

He touched a key tied to the string and drew a spark, then used the charge to fill a Leyden jar. The fullest account of the day comes not from Franklin himself, who never gave precise details of his own experiment, but from Joseph Priestley's history written fifteen years later from what Franklin had told him.

John Walker was mixing chemicals in his shop when a dried lump of his paste, scraped off a stick against his hearth to clean it, burst into flame. He had been trying to make a percussion powder for guns and stumbled onto something else entirely: a stick that lit itself with friction.

He never patented the friction match. Asked why, he said only that he expected it to benefit the public, so people should simply have it. He kept no written record of the exact formula either, and within a few years a chemist named Samuel Jones had copied the idea and sold his own version as the Lucifer match, far more successfully than Walker ever did.

The Wujing Zongyao took a team of Song dynasty scholars five years to compile, led by the official Zeng Gongliang with an astronomer and a court scholar assisting him. Commissioned under Emperor Renzong partly because of conflict with the Western Xia, it covered naval vessels and siege engines alongside its chemistry.

It sets down not one formula but three: a fireball for trebuchets, a caltrop bomb built to snag on wooden structures, and a poisonous smoke ball for chemical attacks. Each mixed saltpetre, sulphur and charcoal with additives like pitch and wax, and the saltpetre content already varied between roughly a third and three fifths by weight.

Taoist alchemists were not looking for a weapon. They were mixing sulphur, charcoal and saltpetre in search of an elixir that would grant eternal life, following methods described as early as the second century by the alchemist Wei Boyang, who warned that some such powders could flare and dance violently.

The Chinese name that stuck, huoyao, translates as fire medicine, a label that still carries the trace of that original purpose. Historians note that the strong link drawn between gunpowder and Taoism may partly reflect which texts happened to survive rather than who actually did the mixing.

Hanno led a Carthaginian fleet, said to number sixty ships, out through the Strait of Gibraltar and down the West African coast, founding settlements along the way. His own account, the Periplus, survives only as an abbreviated Greek translation of the lost Punic original, describing rivers, nomadic tribes and a night sky lit by distant fires.

How far south he got is disputed: estimates range from southern Morocco to as far as Gabon, because the sailing distances he recorded do not match any single coastline well. He also described an island of hairy, aggressive people his interpreters called gorillas, a name later borrowed for the modern ape.

Hero of Alexandria's aeolipile was a sealed sphere mounted over a fire, with two bent nozzles that let escaping steam spin it on its axis. It is the earliest steam turbine on record, built in the first century AD, and it worked exactly as described: heat water, trap the steam, let it push against the air through an angled outlet.

It never became a machine that pulled a load or turned a mill. Rome had cheap labour, no market demanding mechanised output, and metalworking that could not yet hold higher pressures safely, so the aeolipile stayed a lecture-hall demonstration of a principle rather than the start of an industrial engine.

Herodotus set out to record the Greco-Persian Wars before, in his own words, time erased the memory of what both Greeks and non-Greeks had achieved. Nothing in the resulting text can be dated later than about 430 BC, and the work is the earliest surviving Greek prose narrative on this scale, which is why Cicero later called him the father of history.

Not everyone agreed the title was earned. Thucydides, writing soon after, dismissed him as a mere storyteller, and later critics went further, branding him the father of lies for including folk tales and secondhand travellers' reports alongside verified events. Modern historians still read him as part reporter and part collector of good stories.

Earlier scholars had assumed Egyptian hieroglyphs were purely symbolic, each sign standing for an idea rather than a sound. Champollion's breakthrough was to treat the royal names ringed in cartouches, Ptolemy and Cleopatra among them, as phonetic spellings and match their sounds letter by letter against the Greek text alongside them on the Rosetta Stone.

On 14 September 1822, comparing Coptic with a hieroglyphic sign for 'birth' in a text from Abu Simbel, he confirmed the system worked the same way throughout. He is said to have run to his brother's office shouting that he had it, then collapsed. He published the decipherment on 27 September 1822.

Almost nothing about Hippocrates's own life is reliably documented beyond his birth around 460 BC on the island of Kos. What survives of his reputation rests on an idea rather than a biography: that illness came from environment, diet and daily habits, not divine punishment, and could therefore be studied and treated by observation.

The seventy or so treatises known as the Hippocratic Corpus are not confidently his own writing. Most scholars think they were produced by later students and physicians working in his tradition, and later collected and attributed to him as his fame grew, possibly when librarians in Alexandria filed assorted medical texts under his name.

A 2.04 million year old skull from Drimolen in South Africa is the oldest specimen currently assigned to Homo erectus, though most fossils date closer to 1 to 1.8 million years. Within a few hundred thousand years the species had reached Georgia, Indonesia and China, the first hominin known to leave Africa at all, well before modern humans existed.

Fire is harder to pin on it than the old textbook image suggests. Burnt material at Wonderwerk Cave in South Africa is 1.7 million years old, but controlled, everyday fire use does not become common in the archaeological record until 300,000 to 400,000 years ago, long after Homo erectus had spread across three continents. Its Acheulean handaxes, by contrast, are unmistakably its own invention.

Hooke was not looking at anything alive. He sliced a thin sheet of cork and put it under his microscope for a 1665 book called Micrographia, and found the dead tissue was built from tiny walled compartments, packed together with no gaps between them.

The shape reminded him of a monk's dormitory or a honeycomb, so he called the compartments cells, a name that stuck long after biologists worked out what was actually inside living ones. Micrographia's engravings, some folding out larger than the book itself, made his tiny discovery visible to readers who had never looked through a lens.

A horseshoe complete with its nails turned up in the tomb of the Frankish king Childeric I at Tournai, in modern Belgium, dated to the fifth century. Roman writers had described mule shoes centuries earlier, but those were probably hipposandals, leather boots strapped over the hoof rather than iron nailed to it.

Written references to horseshoes are scarcer than the metal itself. The earliest clear mention of crescent shaped irons and their nails dates to 910, and only becomes common in texts after that. On rocky or icy ground a shod horse kept its footing and its hoof wall intact where an unshod one wore down or split.

A sheep, a duck and a rooster went first, sent up over Versailles in September 1783 before Louis XVI to check whether altitude itself was survivable. Two months later, on 21 November, Pilatre de Rozier and the marquis d'Arlandes climbed into a basket beneath a Montgolfier balloon at the Chateau de la Muette and cut loose.

They rose to roughly 900 metres and drifted about nine kilometres across Paris in twenty five minutes, close enough to fires drifting up from the straw-fed burner that embers kept scorching the fabric and Pilatre had to beat them out with a wet sponge. There was fuel left for four or five times the distance when they set the balloon down between two windmills.

Humboldt sailed from La Coruna in June 1799 with the botanist Aime Bonpland, funding the whole venture from his own inheritance. In Venezuela the pair paddled the Orinoco and confirmed a natural channel, the Casiquiare, linking that river's basin to the Amazon's, a connection earlier travellers had doubted existed.

In 1802 they climbed Chimborazo in Ecuador, reaching roughly 5,878 metres before ice and altitude turned them back, then the highest a European had gone. Humboldt's real haul was data: barometric readings, plant collections and notes on colonial economies that took decades to publish and reshaped how geography itself was studied.

Ibn Battuta left Tangier on 14 June 1325, aged twenty one, meaning only to complete the hajj, a pilgrimage to Mecca that usually took sixteen months there and back. He later wrote that an unexplained impulse kept him from turning home once he arrived.

That impulse became three decades on the road through Africa, Asia and the Iberian Peninsula, working along the way as a judge and diplomat. His dictated account, the Rihla, is the reason his roughly 117,000 kilometres of travel are documented at all rather than merely claimed.

Glass began as beads rather than vessels, and they turn up across Mesopotamia, Egypt and the Syrian coast at roughly the same time, in the mid third millennium BCE. No single workshop can claim the invention: the likeliest path is accidental, a byproduct of metal smelting slag or of firing faience, a glazed ceramic that came first.

Deliberate, sustained glass production took far longer to arrive. Mesopotamia was producing glass in quantity by around 1600 BCE, with Egypt following roughly a century later. Both traditions made small, precious objects, colored beads and inlays rather than clear panes, since transparent glass was still centuries away.

The earliest picture of a sail is not Egyptian. A pottery shard from the Ubaid period in the Persian Gulf, roughly 3500 to 3000 BCE, appears to show a boat with twin masts and a sail, several centuries before any known Egyptian image of one.

Egyptian evidence follows at around 3100 BCE, and it is Egypt's boats on the Nile that are best documented, since sail let a crew travel upstream against the current by catching wind rather than rowing the whole distance. Both regions arrived at the same idea early, and which one used it first is a matter of which shard survived.

Iron working did not begin with a single people or a single breakthrough. Small quantities turn up in Central Anatolia by around 1800 BCE, and separately in the Ganges Valley at about the same date, long before iron replaced bronze anywhere at scale. The idea that the Hittites held a guarded monopoly on the technique has not held up under closer study.

Large-scale iron production only became the norm around 1200 BCE, near the end of the Bronze Age, once smiths learned to forge it into tools stronger and cheaper than cast bronze. The shift mattered most when tin, bronze's scarce ingredient, grew hard to get: iron needed no long-distance trade network, only ore that most regions already had.

Lavoisier began by heating phosphorus and sulfur in sealed vessels and weighing them before and after, finding they gained mass rather than losing it, the opposite of what phlogiston theory predicted. He traced that gained weight to a component of air, which he isolated and named oxygen in 1778, from Greek for acid-former.

He then turned to breathing. Memoirs he read to the Academy of Sciences from 1777 argued that an animal consumes the same gas a flame does, and later calorimeter work with Laplace showed a guinea pig produced heat at roughly the rate a burning candle would, given the same volume of oxygen used. Respiration, he concluded, was a slow form of combustion.

Edwin Beard Budding worked at a textile mill and adapted a rotary blade designed for trimming the nap off woollen cloth into a machine that could cut grass to an even height. He patented it on 31 August 1830, insisting on a witness clause in the agreement because he thought the device might look ridiculous enough for people to laugh at him pushing it.

Regent's Park Zoological Gardens and several Oxford colleges bought early machines, and Ransomes began building licensed copies by 1832. The mower made close-cropped turf affordable at scale, and level, evenly cut ground became the standard surface for the football pitches, bowling greens and tennis courts codified later in the century.

Thomas Jefferson sent the Corps of Discovery west within a year of buying the Louisiana Territory, wanting a river route to the Pacific and a record of what he had just bought. Meriwether Lewis and William Clark left near St Louis in May 1804 with about thirty men, working up the Missouri and over the Continental Divide.

Sacagawea, a young Shoshone woman travelling with her infant son and her husband Toussaint Charbonneau, was not the party's guide, but her presence signalled peaceful intent to tribes along the route and her interpreting proved essential. The party reached the Pacific in November 1805 and returned to St Louis in September 1806, having mapped territory no American expedition had crossed before.

Naturalists before Carl Linnaeus described species in sprawling Latin phrases, so a single plant might carry a name running to a dozen words. His Systema Naturae, printed in the Netherlands in 1735, began as a slim twelve pages sorting plants by counting their stamens and pistils.

The system grew enormously over later editions, reaching roughly 4,400 animal species and 7,700 plant species by 1758, and it settled into the two word genus and species naming still used today. Not everyone adopted it at once. The English botanist Philip Miller kept using an older classification for years before switching over.

The oldest known lock was not Egyptian. One was recovered from the ruins of Nineveh in ancient Assyria, and locks of this general age run to more than six thousand years old, well before the wooden pin device usually credited to Egypt.

The Egyptian version worked by gravity: wooden pins dropped into holes drilled through a sliding bolt, jamming it in place, and a key lifted the pins clear so the bolt could move. The same principle, a set of pins held by gravity or a spring until a matching key raises them, still runs the modern Yale lock.

What is written down is not the bow's invention but a witness to it. Around 1188 the churchman Gerald of Wales described the bows of Gwent, made of elm rather than yew, as strong enough for close fighting as well as long shots.

Gerald's proof is a single grim anecdote: a Welsh arrow went through a knight's mail-protected thigh, his leather tunic, his saddle, and killed the horse beneath him. It was that account, not a manufacturer's record, that fixed the weapon's reputation before the English army had adopted it.

Magellan never finished the voyage that carries his name. He was killed on Mactan in the Philippines in April 1521, speared and then cut down on a beach, roughly halfway through the three-year journey he had begun with five ships in September 1519.

Command passed to Juan Sebastian Elcano, who brought the last surviving ship, the Victoria, home to Spain in September 1522. Of about 270 men who set out, only 18 or 19 returned on board her, the sole ship of the original five to complete the full circuit.

No first clock survives. The earliest picture of a weight-driven one is an illustration in the Bible of St Louis, made between 1226 and 1234, showing the fall of the weight slowed by water turning a wheel. No working example from that period survives.

By 1271 the English astronomer Robertus Anglicus wrote that craftsmen were trying to build a wheel that would turn once a day using gravity alone, without yet managing it reliably. The idea combined gearing and striking mechanisms already known from European and Islamic astronomical instruments.

Cyrus McCormick gave the first public demonstration of his reaper in 1831 at Steeles Tavern, Virginia, but it took until 1834 to secure a patent, and even then nobody bought one. Early versions jammed and stalled on uneven ground, and years of quiet redesign passed before the machine could be trusted on a real harvest.

Sales only picked up in the 1840s, once the design had been reworked for varied terrain and crops. By 1856 McCormick's factory was turning out more than four thousand reapers a year, mostly bound for the flat, expanding wheat farms of the American Midwest, and the machine cut the number of hands a farm needed to bring in a harvest.

Alcohol thermometers of the early 1700s drifted and disagreed with each other, since no two instrument makers used the same fixed points. Daniel Gabriel Fahrenheit, who had been building spirit thermometers since around 1706, began working with mercury around 1713 and found it expanded more evenly with heat.

He anchored his scale with three points: a salt and ice mixture at zero, the temperature at which still water starts to freeze at thirty two, and roughly the temperature of the human body near the top. By 1721 his manufacturing was consistent enough that two of his thermometers, made years apart, would finally agree.

Bi Sheng was a commoner about whom almost nothing else is recorded, working in the Song dynasty sometime between 1039 and 1048. He pressed individual characters from sticky clay and fired them hard, so a page could be assembled from reusable type instead of carved fresh on a single block.

He also tried wood, but abandoned it: grain and swelling from ink and moisture warped the letters until they no longer sat flush. Clay type never displaced woodblock printing in China, since carving a full set of characters cost more than simply paying a copyist, and woodblocks remained the everyday choice for centuries after him.

Deep coal seams kept flooding, and horse-driven pumps could not keep up. Thomas Newcomen's engine, raised at the Conygree colliery in Tipton in 1712, used steam to push a piston, then cooled the cylinder with a jet of water so air pressure drove it back down.

It burned through coal at a rate that would have ruined any other buyer, cooling and reheating the same cylinder on every stroke, but a coal mine had fuel to spare at the pithead. Mines kept using Newcomen's design for decades until James Watt's separate condenser roughly doubled its fuel efficiency in 1769.

No falling apple is recorded in Newton's own notebooks from 1666. The story comes from accounts he gave late in life, decades after the fact, and even those describe an apple prompting a thought rather than striking him on the head.

What is documented is that Cambridge closed for plague that year and Newton worked alone at his family home in Woolsthorpe, making early progress on calculus, optics and gravitation at once. He did not publish the finished theory until 1687, in the Principia, after sitting on it for two decades.

Joseph Black had noticed that a candle would not burn inside a jar of carbon dioxide, and he handed the puzzle of what else the air might contain to his student. Rutherford sealed a mouse inside a confined volume of air until it died, then burned a candle and phosphorus in what remained until neither would combust.

What was left would not sustain a flame or an animal, and Rutherford, still working within phlogiston theory, called it noxious air. He took his degree at Edinburgh on the strength of that 1772 thesis, having isolated nitrogen without yet understanding it as a distinct element rather than exhausted, used-up air.

Georg Ohm published his result in 1827, in a book whose title translates as The Galvanic Circuit Investigated Mathematically, setting out how current through a conductor varies with the voltage across it and the resistance it meets. He had reached it by careful bench measurements on wires of different lengths and thicknesses, not by abstract theory.

German physicists mostly ignored the work, and one official dismissed it as heresy against the true spirit of physics. Ohm resigned his teaching post over the reception and spent years without a permanent academic position. Recognition came late: the Royal Society awarded him the Copley Medal in 1841, fourteen years after the law now named for him first appeared in print.

Carl Wilhelm Scheele had already isolated the gas by heating mercuric oxide, three years before Joseph Priestley reached the same result in England in 1774, but Scheele did not publish his findings until 1777. Priestley got there independently, unaware of the earlier work, and called what he found dephlogisticated air.

Neither man understood what he had made. Both were still reasoning within phlogiston theory, which held that burning released a substance rather than combined with one. It was Antoine Lavoisier who worked out that the gas was a distinct element and gave it the name oxygen, from Greek roots meaning acid-former.

Paper already existed before Cai Lun. Fragments bearing legible Chinese writing have been dated to 8 BC, more than a century earlier, and hemp paper had been made for wrapping and padding for centuries before that. What Cai Lun did, as a court official under the Han around 105 AD, was standardise a process that made paper cheap and consistent.

His recipe used mulberry bark and other bast fibres beaten together with old rags, hemp waste and even discarded fishnets, pulped and pressed into thin, even sheets. That combination of cheap, recycled raw material made paper practical to produce at the scale an empire's bureaucracy needed, which is why his name attached to the invention rather than an earlier maker's.

Clocks before 1656 drifted by roughly fifteen minutes a day, close enough for a household but useless for astronomy or navigation. Huygens, working from Galileo's earlier observation that a swinging weight keeps a steady beat, worked out how to couple a pendulum to a clock's escapement so each swing released the gears by a fixed amount.

He had the clockmaker Salomon Coster build the design in Christmas week of 1656 and patented it the following year. The new clocks lost or gained only about fifteen seconds a day, roughly sixty times better than before, which made timekeeping precise enough to be genuinely useful for scientific work.

Herodotus, writing over a century later, said Pharaoh Necho II sent Phoenician sailors from the Red Sea to round the whole African coast and return through the Mediterranean. The crew supposedly took three years, landing each autumn to sow grain and wait for the harvest before sailing on.

Herodotus himself did not believe one detail: the sailors reported the sun on their right hand as they sailed west along Africa's southern coast. To anyone south of the equator that is exactly where the sun sits at midday, a fact no Mediterranean sailor could have known in advance, which is why some historians treat the doubted detail as the strongest evidence the voyage happened.

Atahualpa brought perhaps 6,000 men to the plaza at Cajamarca in November 1532, unarmed for a ceremonial reception. Pizarro's force numbered under 200, with only a few dozen horses and a handful of primitive guns, and the emperor saw no reason to fear them.

A friar demanded he accept Christian teaching and pay tribute to a foreign king. Atahualpa refused, and the Spanish opened fire from ambush, killing thousands of his retinue and capturing him within hours. He filled rooms with gold and silver as ransom, then was executed the following year on charges his captors invented.

Before any plough, farmers broke ground with digging sticks and hoes, a slow method suited to the narrow flood strips along rivers like the Nile. The ard, a simple wooden blade dragged by oxen to scratch a furrow rather than turn the soil, followed animal domestication and let one team work far more land than hand tools allowed.

The clearest early trace is not a tool but a field: ploughed furrows preserved at Kalibangan in the Indus Valley, dated to around 2800 BCE, alongside a terracotta model that shows the ard's shape. Egyptian tomb paintings and Akkadian seals from roughly the same broad period confirm the design spread across several early farming regions rather than starting in one place.

The Lapita culture, working from island Southeast Asia, had reached Tonga and Samoa by roughly 900 BCE after crossing some 6,000 kilometres of open Pacific in outrigger canoes. From there, expansion paused for over a thousand years before pushing on to the Cook Islands and the Society Islands, with Hawaii, Easter Island and New Zealand settled later still.

None of it used instruments. Navigators memorised a fixed sequence of rising and setting stars for each route and read the ocean itself: swell direction, cloud shapes over distant land, and the flight paths of birds that returned to shore each evening. That knowledge passed from a master navigator to an apprentice by song, not by chart.

Ponce de Leon sighted land on 2 April 1513 during Easter season and named it La Florida for its green coastline, having sailed out of Puerto Rico in search of new territory rather than treasure already claimed by others. The fountain of youth attached to his name has no basis in any account written in his lifetime; it was added by writers after his death.

He returned to colonise Florida in 1521 and was wounded in the thigh by an arrow during fighting with local Calusa people. He sailed for Cuba and died there within weeks; his remains were later moved to a cathedral tomb in San Juan.

Joseph Aspdin, a Leeds bricklayer, patented his cement in 1824 and named it after Portland stone, the pale limestone quarried on Dorset's Isle of Portland and used on buildings such as St Paul's Cathedral. He wanted builders to associate his grey powder with that admired, expensive stone before they had even used it.

His actual product was not what later got sold under the same name. Chemists now call it proto-Portland cement, a rougher forerunner burned at lower temperatures than the real thing. It was Aspdin's son William who, working through the 1840s, raised the kiln heat enough to form the calcium silicates that make modern Portland cement so strong.

No one lived on the Cape Verde islands before Portuguese ships found them around 1456. Portugal's own records credit the Genoese-born navigator Antonio de Noli, though Diogo Gomes and Alvise Cadamosto also sailed the coast in the same years and each has been given some claim to the discovery.

Afonso V made Noli governor of the islands he had found, and Portuguese settlers followed. Lying off the West African coast on the Atlantic trade winds, the empty archipelago became one of the earliest European settlements built entirely outside Europe.

Japan does not hold the oldest known pottery. China does, in fragments from Xianren Cave in Jiangxi province dated to roughly 20,000 to 19,000 years ago. Japan's own early tradition, the Jomon, follows later, with earthenware from the Odai Yamamoto site dated to around 14,500 BCE, still thousands of years before farming reached the region.

These first pots were not for storing grain, since nobody was yet growing any. Weights for fishing nets are one common early use, and Jomon vessels show signs of use in processing freshwater and marine food, likely for storage rather than cooking. Firing clay to make a shape permanent came long before anyone needed a jar for a harvest.

Dyed cloth carried woodblock patterns in China before the technique reached paper. The oldest securely dated printed text to survive is a copy of the Diamond Sutra, a Buddhist scripture, whose colophon gives the exact day it was produced: the 11th of May, 868, made for free distribution on behalf of a family's parents.

Carving a block took skill, but printing from it needed none: once cut, a single block could stamp thousands of identical pages. By the Song dynasty, that had cut the price of a book to roughly a tenth of what a hand copied one had cost, spreading texts to readers who had never owned one.

Ptolemy finished his astronomical treatise around 150 AD after roughly a quarter century of observation from Alexandria. Across thirteen books he set out spherical trigonometry, models for the sun, moon and five known planets, and a catalogue listing 1,022 stars sorted into 48 constellations, all built on the assumption that the earth sat still at the centre.

That earth-centred model was wrong, but the mathematics describing what the sky actually does was good enough to predict eclipses and planetary positions for over a thousand years. Arabic scholars translated it in the ninth century, Latin Europe in the twelfth, and it remained the working reference until the Scientific Revolution replaced it.

Babylonian scribes were using the relationship between the sides of a right triangle over a thousand years before Pythagoras was born. A clay tablet known as Plimpton 322, dated to around 1800 BC, lists fifteen sets of the whole numbers the theorem produces, and Egyptian and Indian texts show similar knowledge long before Greece.

No surviving Greek text from the five centuries after Pythagoras's life credits him personally with a proof. Later writers such as Cicero and Plutarch attributed the theorem to him as though the link were already common knowledge, and that later tradition, not a documented proof, is why his name has stayed attached to it.

Pytheas was the first Mediterranean sailor known to have reached Britain, and he claimed to have gone further still, six days' sail north to a land he called Thule where the sun barely set in summer. He also linked the tides to the phases of the moon, an idea Mediterranean sailors had not needed before because their own sea barely tides at all.

His original account survives only in quotations by later writers, and the geographer Strabo dismissed him outright as a liar. Modern historians take a softer view: the midnight sun and the strange half-solid, half-liquid sea he described drifting with ice sound less like invention and more like a real, garbled encounter with the Arctic.

Appius Claudius Caecus, the censor better remembered for the road that carries his name, began the Aqua Appia in 312 BC. It ran for about 16.6 kilometres yet dropped only around 10 metres over that whole distance, a slope engineers had to hold almost dead level using nothing but sightlines and levels.

Nearly all of it ran underground rather than on arches, which kept the water cool and the channel harder to poison or sabotage. By the end of the 1st century BC it had stopped carrying drinking water into Rome and was reused instead as part of the city's sewer network.

Roman builders mixed lime with pozzolana, volcanic ash from around the Bay of Naples, to make a mortar that could set underwater, something no other ancient mortar could do. Vitruvius recorded the ratios: one part lime to three of pozzolana for buildings, one to two for harbour work.

In 2023 researchers found that the lumps of unmixed lime long dismissed as sloppy workmanship were deliberate. Mixed hot rather than slaked first, the lime left reactive clasts that dissolve into cracks and reseal them with fresh calcium carbonate, a self-repair that helped piers and domes such as the Pantheon's survive two thousand years of weather.

Lieutenant Pierre-Francois Bouchard was not looking for antiquities. His men were demolishing a wall at Fort Julien near Rosetta in July 1799 when they turned up a slab of dark granodiorite carved with three scripts stacked one above the other.

Two of the three texts, Greek and Egyptian demotic, were readable at once and gave scholars a crib for the third, hieroglyphic. Thomas Young worked out that some signs were phonetic; Jean-Francois Champollion finished the decipherment in Paris in 1822, after the stone itself had been surrendered to Britain and shipped to the British Museum.

The earliest scissors were not the pivoted kind familiar today. Spring scissors used two bronze blades joined by a thin curved strip of metal, so squeezing the handles together did the cutting and the metal's own springiness pulled the blades back open. Both Egypt and Mesopotamia produced versions of this design in the Bronze Age, and which came first is not settled.

The pivoted design, a fixed screw or rivet joining two blades that cross like a modern pair of scissors, is a much later Roman refinement; shears of that type recovered at Trabzon date to the second century CE. Pivoted scissors were not manufactured in large numbers until factories in Sheffield began producing them in 1761.

Scattering seed by hand wasted much of it and left rows uneven, since a good third could land too shallow, too deep or on top of another seed entirely. Jethro Tull's drill, drawn by a horse, cut a furrow, dropped seed at a set depth and covered it in one pass.

Tull was not first: Chinese multi-tube drills date to the second century BCE, and a Venetian patent for one was granted in 1566. What Tull's version did, from 1701 on his Berkshire farm, was cut seed use while raising yield enough that English landowners began copying it within his lifetime.

Finding a ship's position at sea meant measuring the angle between a star and the horizon from a deck that never stopped moving, and older instruments like the backstaff forced the navigator to face away from the star to read it. A reflecting instrument with mirrors solved that, letting the observer view both at once.

John Hadley in London and Thomas Godfrey in Philadelphia arrived at essentially the same design around 1731, apparently without knowledge of each other's work. Isaac Newton had sketched the same principle decades earlier, but he never published it, so the credit went to the two men who built working instruments.

Tradition credits an indigenous prospector, Diego Huallpa, with finding the silver seam at Cerro Rico in 1545 while chasing a stray llama up the mountain. Whatever the truth of the story, a Spanish mining town grew around the site fast enough that a saying entered the language: valer un Potosi, to be worth a fortune.

By the late 1500s the mountain was supplying an estimated 60 percent of the world's silver, carried out by llama and mule train to Pacific ports before crossing to Spain or on to Asia through the Manila galleons. Potosi's population passed 200,000, briefly making it one of the largest cities on earth.

A Sumerian clay tablet of roughly 2500 BCE gives a recipe for a soap-like paste made by heating oil with wood ash, one of the oldest chemical reactions ever written down. It was not made for bathing. The record ties it to washing wool, cleaning cloth rather than skin.

Similar oil-and-alkali mixtures turn up in Babylonian and Egyptian texts over the following centuries, but a soap with the properties recognisable today did not settle into use until much later, around the first century CE. The Babylonian formula is the earliest fixed point, not the finished product.

Weaving had raced ahead of spinning. John Kay's flying shuttle let one weaver work faster than several spinners could feed him yarn, and Crompton set out to close the gap by combining Arkwright's water frame with Hargreaves's spinning jenny, producing a machine that could draw yarn fine and strong enough for warp or weft alike.

He could not afford the fees to patent the design in 1779, so he sold the rights to a Scottish manufacturer, David Dale, who patented the mule and profited from it while Crompton went back to weaving for a living. Within decades the mule was spinning most of Britain's cotton, without ever paying its inventor for it.

Nobody can pin the spinning wheel to one workshop. Candidates include India, China and the Middle East, and the clearest early illustrations, from Baghdad around 1237 and China around 1270, postdate the claimed origins by centuries, leaving the earliest history to guesswork rather than surviving pictures.

Wherever it began, its effect was not in doubt: turning a wheel to twist fibre into thread was more than ten times faster than spinning by hand with a drop spindle. The wheel reached Europe by the thirteenth century and underpinned cotton and wool textile production for five hundred years before mechanised spinning replaced it.

On 21 February 1804 a locomotive built by Richard Trevithick hauled five wagons along the tramway of the Penydarren ironworks in Merthyr Tydfil, Wales, carrying ten tons of iron and about seventy men who had wagered it could not be done. It covered roughly sixteen kilometres in just over four hours, at a walking pace.

The run proved the principle but broke the tramway: the cast iron plates had been laid for horse traffic and cracked under the engine's weight. Rather than rebuild the line, the ironworks put the locomotive back to its old job driving a hammer, and railways stayed horse drawn for another two decades before the idea returned in a stronger form.

A Western Jin tomb near Changsha held a small clay figurine of a rider whose foot rests in a mounting stirrup, dated to around 302. It shows a single stirrup, used only for climbing into the saddle, not yet the paired kind that supports both feet while riding.

The earliest reliably dated paired stirrups come from a Northern Yan noble's tomb of 415, made of gilded mulberry wood reinforced with bronze and iron. Once a rider had both feet braced, a lance could be couched under the arm and driven forward with the horse's full weight, reshaping mounted combat across Eurasia.

Egypt supplies the oldest sundial recovered from the ground, a shadow clock from the Valley of the Kings dated to around 1500 BCE, roughly matching the earliest Babylonian devices of the same kind. It worked by casting a shadow across a marked bar rather than a dial, so the shape looked nothing like the round clock face people now picture.

Both Egyptian and Babylonian astronomers were using the sun's shadow to break the day into set intervals at roughly the same period, and neither tradition can be shown to have borrowed the idea from the other. The devices improved over the following centuries, but the underlying principle, a fixed object casting a moving shadow, never changed.

Tasman never saw mainland Australia on this voyage. He sighted the island he named Van Diemen's Land, after the Dutch East India Company official who sent him, on 24 November 1642, then sailed on to New Zealand without landing on either.

Off New Zealand's coast three weeks later, a Maori waka rammed a boat ferrying men between Tasman's two ships, killing four sailors. Tasman sailed away without ever setting foot ashore and called the bay Murderers' Bay. Van Diemen's Land was not renamed Tasmania until the following century.

Herodotus wrote that Thales foretold the solar eclipse that stopped a battle between the Lydians and the Medes, so unnerving both armies that they made peace on the spot. Astronomers have matched the story to the eclipse of 28 May 585 BC, which reached totality over Anatolia.

Whether Thales actually predicted it is doubted. He had no access to the Babylonian records that could have let him calculate a specific eclipse, and Herodotus's own chronology puts the Median king in the story ten years dead by 585 BC. Some historians think the tale originally described a lunar eclipse instead, which ancient observers could forecast far more reliably.

Well engineers had a puzzle: no suction pump could lift water higher than about ten metres, whatever the design. Galileo blamed a limited force of vacuum pulling the water up. Torricelli suspected something pressing down from outside instead, and tested the idea with a liquid dense enough to fit the whole apparatus on a bench.

In 1643 he filled a metre-long glass tube with mercury, sealed one end, and inverted it into a mercury-filled basin. The column fell to about 76 centimetres, leaving an empty space above it, now called a Torricellian vacuum. The weight of the surrounding air, he reasoned, was pushing the mercury up the tube from the basin below.

Shockley's name is on the Nobel Prize but not on the first patent. Bardeen and Brattain built the working device on 16 December 1947, a sliver of germanium touched by two gold contacts a hair's width apart, and theirs alone are the names on the point contact patent Bell Labs was awarded for it the following year.

Stung at having missed the breakthrough, Shockley spent New Year's Eve 1947 sketching a rival design in a Chicago hotel room during a physics conference, then had the design worked out back in New Jersey by the end of January 1948. Bell Labs later licensed the patents free of royalties to hearing aid makers, a nod to founder Alexander Graham Bell, and hearing aids became the first product built on it.

Nobody can say with confidence where the counterweight trebuchet was first built. The earliest description of one comes from a military writer in 1187, and the design seems to have spread across Muslim and Christian lands around the Mediterranean before the Mongols carried it on to China in the following century.

Its predecessor, the traction trebuchet, needed a crew hauling ropes on the short end of the beam. The counterweight version replaced them with a huge box of stone or sand that fell under its own weight, trading a slower reload for far greater force: reconstructions have thrown an eight kilogram stone well over four hundred metres.

William Austin Burt, a Michigan surveyor, patented a writing machine he called the typographer in 1829, years before the word typewriter existed. It printed one letter at a time from a wheel that had to be rotated by hand to the right character before each keystroke, which made it slower than writing by pen.

The London Science Museum later called it the first writing machine whose invention is documented, a careful phrase that concedes earlier attempts existed without records to prove it. Burt's machine never reached the market. Practical, sellable typewriters would not appear for another four decades.

Da Gama left Lisbon on 8 July 1497 and reached Calicut on the Malabar coast on 20 May 1498, a ten-month voyage that opened the first all-sea route between Europe and India. The gifts he brought for the local ruler, the Zamorin, were cloth, hats and coral, and they were judged too poor for a royal ambassador.

Muslim merchants already trading in Calicut told the Zamorin the newcomers were pirates, and da Gama could not meet a customs demand paid in gold. He left without an agreement and without permission to station a representative, taking several local men with him by force.

A farmer digging in a walled field on Milos in April 1820 uncovered the statue in two pieces. A French naval officer with an interest in antiquity, Olivier Voutier, was on the island and urged him to keep clearing the ground rather than stop at the first find.

A marble hand holding an apple turned up nearby and, by most reconstructions, belonged to the same figure, suggesting she once held the fruit in one hand while the other steadied her slipping drapery. French diplomats bought the statue before rival buyers could secure it, and Louis XVIII had it placed in the Louvre in 1821, arms already missing.

For over a thousand years, European anatomy had rested on Galen, who had dissected pigs and apes rather than people and assumed the results carried across. Vesalius opened human cadavers himself in 1543 and found Galen wrong on basics: the jaw is one bone, not two, and the breastbone has three parts, not seven.

His seven-volume Fabrica, printed in Basel, paired those corrections with roughly 273 plates showing flayed figures posed against landscapes, their skin and muscle peeled back layer by layer. Who drew them is still argued over, with a pupil of Titian's the leading but unproven candidate. Vesalius insisted the point was the dissecting, not the drawing.

The sagas credit Leif Erikson with the voyage, sailing after Bjarni Herjolfsson had already sighted an unknown coast without landing on it. The only confirmed Norse site in the Americas is L'Anse aux Meadows in Newfoundland, found in the 1960s by Anne Stine and Helge Ingstad, with a cloak pin, iron working debris and boat repair tools among its finds.

Tree rings from timber felled at the site let researchers date the Norse presence there with unusual precision. It was not a colony meant to last: the buildings suited an overwintering base and ship repair station, housing at most a few dozen people rather than a permanent settlement.

Erik the Red was not exploring by choice. Outlawed from Iceland for killing a neighbour's kinsman after a feud that began with a landslide, he spent his three years of banishment charting the coast of an unknown land to the west, returning to Iceland once the exile ended.
